coreStoryFacts.text: SINGAPORE/TOKYO Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets.

TRM said the attackers were able to order wallets that Binance uses to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to North Korea.

World Liberty Financial said it ​worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder ​Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.

BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to CoinGecko, while shaky ​confidence ​hit listed crypto exchange shares.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, ​has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses.
"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance ‌said in a post on X.
"Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said.
Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach.

Mark Karpeles, former chief of defunct Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox, which collapsed a dozen years ago after $500 million in bitcoin was stolen, said attackers probably accessed private keys for at least two Binance wallets.
"Binance appears to have split its assets across multiple systems, ensuring a hack can only affect a part of the assets, but even so a single hack is a large loss," he said.
"It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said as crypto prices fell broadly.

An initial investigation suggested the breach ‌may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
Crypto exchange Binance has suffered a $6.3 billion hack, the largest to hit the digital-asset industry and the latest in a slew of security incidents afflicting the financial sector.
The world’s largest crypto trading platform suspended all withdrawals Friday and pledged to cover all losses.
Binance has temporarily suspended all withdrawals, which it expects to resume within 48 hours, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X.
The company said it will cover all losses and “user funds are safe.”
Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost US$1.5 billion of tokens.
For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident is a potential setback.
[NEW YORK] Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, said US$6.3 billion of funds are involved in what the industry is describing as crypto’s biggest-ever hack.
“The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data.

“Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.”

[NEW YORK] Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, said US$6.3 billion of funds are involved in what the industry is describing as crypto’s biggest-ever hack. Digital tokens fell.

“The estimated total impact sits at around US$6.3 billion,” Binance said in a post on X. “We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~US$3 billion frozen on-chain so far.”

Binance has temporarily suspended all withdrawals, which it expects to resume within 48 hours, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X. The company said it will cover all losses and “user funds are safe.”
Blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs said North Korea was behind the heist, which it called “the largest crypto theft on record.”
“TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” the firm said. “We make this judgment with high confidence.”

Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost US$1.5 billion of tokens. For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident is a potential setback.
Five decades of milestones and moments that shaped Singapore’s success story - told through our headlines.
Bitcoin dropped 3 per cent at the end of the US session and a further 3 per cent in Asia trading, falling below US$77,000 to its lowest level since September, with other tokens also selling off.

“The rumored Binance hack is definitely driving down coin prices,” said Fredrick Collins, chief executive and co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data. “Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI.”

The hackers appear to have exploited how Binance authorises transactions, according to TRM. They seemingly gained access to the exchange’s systems and used internal software to authorise transfers across 10 different blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, it said.
Binance said the incident may involve a compromised software engineer’s laptop. “We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak,” the company said.

An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) was established in 2018 to serve a backstop for customers in “extreme situations,” according to the exchange.
The SAFU is generally maintained at around US$1 billion, but has fluctuated in the past in tandem with market movements, Binance said in 2024.

The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze missing currency. Paolo Ardoino, the chief executive officer of Tether, said in an X post that it froze more than US$1.5 billion of the stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack.”
Jeremy Allaire, who runs Circle Internet Group, said US$800 million of its coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit involving Binance.”

Sentiment was already fragile after a spate of crypto security incidents. In recent months, hundreds of millions of dollars were drained from Bitget , while tampering tied to Ledger devices also led to millions of dollars in losses.

“Attackers are operating at unprecedented speed and scale” but “the tools to track and trace operate at that speed too,” said Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “Stablecoin issuers freeze within hours. Investigators follow funds across chains in real time.”
Traders had already been bracing for greater volatility in the crypto market this week, with US$11 billion in options set to expire on Friday.

This comes days ahead of the US midterm elections taking place next week, when Democrats could potentially retake one or both chambers of Congress and open the door to greater regulatory scrutiny for the industry.
Exchange thefts and malfeasance have been an ever-present backdrop of crypto’s almost two-decade ascent, the most famous of which was the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in November 2022.

In what remains perhaps the most notorious hacking incident, Japan-based Bitcoin exchange Mt. Gox was struck in 2011. Over time, the hackers made off with tokens worth billions of dollars based on the current market price. Mt. Gox eventually went bankrupt.

“It’s a huge damage to crypto because of the consistent successful hacks in the space,” said Tian Zeng, chief executive officer of crypto hedge fund Third Eye. “The fact that exploits keep happening makes it dangerous in the age of newest AI models being released every two weeks.”
The Binance incident came on the same day event-contract venue Polymarket halted trading on its international exchange for an hour after it said that a third-party software provider was compromised.
More than 700 Polymarket users were drained of US$2.7 million in funds, said blockchain analytics platform Bubblemaps, in a post on X. A spokesman declined to comment on the numbers.

Recent security incidents haven’t been confined to crypto firms. South Korea’s Daishin Securities disclosed a data leak affecting about 38,000 customers this week, and Mirae Asset Global Investments reported a hacking incident, Yonhap reported.

passages: Hackers stole approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from wallets held at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators have described as the biggest crypto heist on record.

Blockchain analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea's elite hacking unit, while Binance has said it will cover all losses and that user funds are safe.The attack involved the movement of funds across 10 blockchains, with most of the cryptocurrency transferred in about 20 minutes, according to US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.

A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had 'high confidence' North Korea was behind the attack.However, the attribution remains an assessment by private intelligence firms and has not been independently established as a confirmed finding by law enforcement.North Korean hacking groups have repeatedly been accused of stealing cryptocurrency and targeting financial institutions.

The exchange has found no evidence so far that a wallet private key was leaked.The exchange also said it had 'temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds'.Binance said it was working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter was handled appropriately.

Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence said its assessment followed an analysis of transactions associated with the hack and comparisons with previous incidents involving the North Korean cyber unit.'Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]' led to the attribution, an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence told CNN.Chainalysis, another cryptocurrency-tracing firm, said it was monitoring the stolen funds as they moved across multiple blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.

extraction.body: [Sportschosun reporter Jang Jong-ho] A North Korean hacking group has been named as being behind a reported hack of Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in which crypto assets worth more than 8 trillion won were stolen. If confirmed, it would be the largest hack in the history of the crypto asset industry. According to foreign media outlets including Reuters and CNN, U.S. blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said in a blog post on the 30th (local time) that TraderTraitor, a North Korean elite hacking group, was behind the security incident at Binance. TRM Labs said its assessment was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain information and that it had a high degree of confidence in its conclusion. According to TRM Labs, on the 29th the attacker transferred crypto assets worth about $6.36 billion (approximately 8.5 trillion won) out of wallets on 10 blockchains held by Binance. A substantial portion of the funds was drained in about 20 minutes. The losses in this incident are at least four times the $1.5 billion lost in the Bybit hack in February 2025. The attack method was also reportedly sophisticated. TRM Labs said the hacker used a new Ethereum feature to modify Binance’s wallets so they could be controlled at will, then used prearranged authorizations to siphon funds from Ethereum and nine other networks while disguising the transfers as legitimate. Citing valid signatures from wallets across several blockchains within a short period, TRM Labs raised the possibility that Binance’s hot-wallet signing system had been compromised. Binance, however, has not yet determined the specific method of intrusion or the cause of the incident. In an official announcement that day, Binance estimated the losses from the security incident at about $6.3 billion. The staggering theft surpasses all previous crypto hacks and nearly doubles the total amount North Korea stole in digital heists last year. Bybit, which claims to be the world’s second-largest cryptocurrency exchange with over 40 million users, was hit on Friday. Within minutes, hackers drained a significant portion of North Korea’s estimated annual GDP. By the weekend, they had already laundered $160 million through a network of accounts linked to North Korean operatives, according to crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs, as reported by American outlet, CNN . Experts warn that Pyongyang’s elite hacking units have become a crucial financial lifeline for the heavily sanctioned regime, helping fund its nuclear and missile programs. Reports from the United Nations and private firms indicate that North Korean hackers have stolen billions from banks and crypto platforms in recent years. In 2023, a White House official revealed that roughly half of North Korea’s missile program funding came from these cyber thefts. Nick Carlsen, a former FBI intelligence analyst specialising in North Korea, described the scale of the Bybit hack as unprecedented. “The ability of these illicit financial networks to absorb such huge amounts of money so quickly is deeply concerning,” he said. Despite the massive loss, Bybit CEO Ben Zhou assured users that the exchange remains solvent and can cover the stolen funds. In a statement, the company confirmed that it is working closely with regulators and law enforcement agencies to address the hack. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the heist, while CNN has reached out to the North Korean embassy in London for a response. Recovering stolen cryptocurrency remains a race against time. Once North Korean operatives steal funds, they quickly move them through a complex web of digital currency swaps before converting them into US dollars or Chinese yuan. Law enforcement agents monitoring these transactions often have mere minutes to intercept the funds. Investigators have so far managed to claw back only a fraction of the stolen money. Crypto security experts reported recovering $43 million, while Tom Robinson, co-founder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, said an additional $243,000 had been seized. “A drop in the ocean, but a start,” Robinson noted. Bybit has offered a 10% reward to any security experts who help retrieve stolen funds. The Bybit hack serves as an early test for how the Trump administration will handle North Korea’s growing reliance on cybercrime. Carlsen warned that current efforts to stop North Korean hackers are failing. “The strategy from governments and industry clearly isn’t working,” he said. “People should be going back to the drawing board right now on how to deter and punish North Korea for these hacks.” With cyber theft proving to be a powerful financial weapon for North Korea, global law enforcement agencies now face mounting pressure to step up their fight against Pyongyang’s cybercriminal network. coreStoryFacts.text: The world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Binance, has been hit by a cyberattack affecting an estimated $6.3 billion in digital assets, the company said.
Blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to North Korean hackers belonging to the TraderTraitor group.

Binance said on X late Thursday that users' funds remained "safe" and that it would cover all losses from the "security incident." Working with blockchain partners, the exchange had so far frozen affected cryptocurrency assets worth around $3 billion, it added.
They currently held cryptocurrencies worth around $2.4 billion that their issuers were unable to access, the firm added.

Hackers stole approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from wallets held at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators have described as the biggest crypto heist on record.

Blockchain analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea's elite hacking unit, while Binance has said it will cover all losses and that user funds are safe.The attack involved the movement of funds across 10 blockchains, with most of the cryptocurrency transferred in about 20 minutes, according to US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.

A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had 'high confidence' North Korea was behind the attack.However, the attribution remains an assessment by private intelligence firms and has not been independently established as a confirmed finding by law enforcement.North Korean hacking groups have repeatedly been accused of stealing cryptocurrency and targeting financial institutions.

The exchange has found no evidence so far that a wallet private key was leaked.The exchange also said it had 'temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds'.Binance said it was working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter was handled appropriately.

Binance said on X late Thursday that users' funds remained "safe" and that it would cover all losses from the "security incident." Working with blockchain partners, the exchange had so far frozen affected cryptocurrency assets worth around $3 billion, it added.
They currently held cryptocurrencies worth around $2.4 billion that their issuers were unable to access, the firm added.

sources.title: $6.3 billion gone, North Korea 'link': Inside the crypto heist at world's largest exchange Binance
passages: Hackers stole approximately $6.36 billion in cryptocurrency from wallets held at Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, in what investigators have described as the biggest crypto heist on record.

Blockchain analysis firms have attributed the attack to North Korea's elite hacking unit, while Binance has said it will cover all losses and that user funds are safe.The attack involved the movement of funds across 10 blockchains, with most of the cryptocurrency transferred in about 20 minutes, according to US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.

A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had 'high confidence' North Korea was behind the attack.However, the attribution remains an assessment by private intelligence firms and has not been independently established as a confirmed finding by law enforcement.North Korean hacking groups have repeatedly been accused of stealing cryptocurrency and targeting financial institutions.

The exchange has found no evidence so far that a wallet private key was leaked.The exchange also said it had 'temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while security checks are completed; revoked the affected address authorization; [and] engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds'.Binance said it was working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter was handled appropriately.

Singapore-based Pangolin Intelligence said its assessment followed an analysis of transactions associated with the hack and comparisons with previous incidents involving the North Korean cyber unit.'Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents [involving the North Korean cyber unit]' led to the attribution, an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence told CNN.Chainalysis, another cryptocurrency-tracing firm, said it was monitoring the stolen funds as they moved across multiple blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.

extraction.body: [Sportschosun reporter Jang Jong-ho] A North Korean hacking group has been named as being behind a reported hack of Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, in which crypto assets worth more than 8 trillion won were stolen. If confirmed, it would be the largest hack in the history of the crypto asset industry. According to foreign media outlets including Reuters and CNN, U.S. blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said in a blog post on the 30th (local time) that TraderTraitor, a North Korean elite hacking group, was behind the security incident at Binance. TRM Labs said its assessment was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain information and that it had a high degree of confidence in its conclusion. According to TRM Labs, on the 29th the attacker transferred crypto assets worth about $6.36 billion (approximately 8.5 trillion won) out of wallets on 10 blockchains held by Binance. A substantial portion of the funds was drained in about 20 minutes. The losses in this incident are at least four times the $1.5 billion lost in the Bybit hack in February 2025. The attack method was also reportedly sophisticated. TRM Labs said the hacker used a new Ethereum feature to modify Binance’s wallets so they could be controlled at will, then used prearranged authorizations to siphon funds from Ethereum and nine other networks while disguising the transfers as legitimate. Citing valid signatures from wallets across several blockchains within a short period, TRM Labs raised the possibility that Binance’s hot-wallet signing system had been compromised. Binance, however, has not yet determined the specific method of intrusion or the cause of the incident. In an official announcement that day, Binance estimated the losses from the security incident at about $6.3 billion. It said initial findings suggested that a laptop belonging to an employee responsible for development and operations had been hacked, allowing the attacker to access an internal service container and use it to execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions. It added that it had found no evidence that the wallets’ private keys had been leaked. Binance said it was tracking the affected assets with partners in the blockchain industry and had frozen assets worth about $3 billion so far. It said users’ assets were safe and pledged to fully cover any losses using its SAFU fund and company funds. It also said it would work with law enforcement to identify the attacker and pursue legal accountability. The basis for TRM Labs’ attribution to North Korea was traces resembling those found in previous North Korea-linked hacks. The group reportedly withdrew small amounts from the anonymizing service Tornado Cash before the attack to fund attack wallets, spent a long time preparing before carrying out the theft, and then executed signatures obtained in advance all at once. This resembled methods observed in the 2025 Bybit hack and the Kelp DAO hack in April 2026. TRM Labs said the money-laundering methods in this incident differed from those used in the Bybit hack. In that incident, bridge services linking the movement of assets between blockchains were used mainly; in this case, large-scale swaps through market makers and asset conversions using lending protocols were more prominent, the firm said. extraction.body: North Korean hackers have pulled off the largest cryptocurrency heist in history, stealing $1.5 billion from “Bybit”, a major crypto exchange, according to security experts. The staggering theft surpasses all previous crypto hacks and nearly doubles the total amount North Korea stole in digital heists last year. Bybit, which claims to be the world’s second-largest cryptocurrency exchange with over 40 million users, was hit on Friday. Within minutes, hackers drained a significant portion of North Korea’s estimated annual GDP. By the weekend, they had already laundered $160 million through a network of accounts linked to North Korean operatives, according to crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs, as reported by American outlet, CNN . Experts warn that Pyongyang’s elite hacking units have become a crucial financial lifeline for the heavily sanctioned regime, helping fund its nuclear and missile programs. Reports from the United Nations and private firms indicate that North Korean hackers have stolen billions from banks and crypto platforms in recent years. In 2023, a White House official revealed that roughly half of North Korea’s missile program funding came from these cyber thefts. Nick Carlsen, a former FBI intelligence analyst specialising in North Korea, described the scale of the Bybit hack as unprecedented. “The ability of these illicit financial networks to absorb such huge amounts of money so quickly is deeply concerning,” he said. Despite the massive loss, Bybit CEO Ben Zhou assured users that the exchange remains solvent and can cover the stolen funds. In a statement, the company confirmed that it is working closely with regulators and law enforcement agencies to address the hack. An FBI spokesperson declined to comment on the heist, while CNN has reached out to the North Korean embassy in London for a response. Recovering stolen cryptocurrency remains a race against time. Once North Korean operatives steal funds, they quickly move them through a complex web of digital currency swaps before converting them into US dollars or Chinese yuan. Law enforcement agents monitoring these transactions often have mere minutes to intercept the funds. Investigators have so far managed to claw back only a fraction of the stolen money. Crypto security experts reported recovering $43 million, while Tom Robinson, co-founder of crypto-tracing firm Elliptic, said an additional $243,000 had been seized. “A drop in the ocean, but a start,” Robinson noted. Bybit has offered a 10% reward to any security experts who help retrieve stolen funds. The Bybit hack serves as an early test for how the Trump administration will handle North Korea’s growing reliance on cybercrime. Carlsen warned that current efforts to stop North Korean hackers are failing. “The strategy from governments and industry clearly isn’t working,” he said. “People should be going back to the drawing board right now on how to deter and punish North Korea for these hacks.” With cyber theft proving to be a powerful financial weapon for North Korea, global law enforcement agencies now face mounting pressure to step up their fight against Pyongyang’s cybercriminal network. passages: The post Binance's $6.3 Billion Hack: North Korea Linked to Record Theft as Exchange Freezes $3 Billion appeared first on ccn.com .
The reported totals reflect different snapshots.
TRM counted approximately $2.7 billion frozen as of 00:30 UTC on October 30, while Binance subsequently reported about $3 billion.
TRM Labs and Chainalysis linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group.
The world's largest crypto exchange said approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen onchain.
It temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigators examined how an attacker gained access to its withdrawal infrastructure.
Binance's preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
The exchange said the attacker may have used that access to enter a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
Other affected wallets transferred assets through ordinary signed transactions.
Fundstrat's Sean Farrell told CNBC the breach did not currently appear to create a significant solvency threat.
His assessment depended partly on the eventual recovery of frozen assets and Binance's ability to absorb the remaining losses.
TRM estimated the theft at $6.36 billion, with most transfers occurring within roughly 20 minutes.
Withdrawal access now represents a critical test.
A smooth reopening could support confidence in Binance's liquidity, while prolonged restrictions could deepen uncertainty.
Binance said it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys.
It has revoked the affected address authorization and promised a technical account once investigators establish the facts.
A batch of 50 previously signed authorizations enabled a malicious contract to take control of a Binance hot wallet and repeatedly drain incoming funds.
It also pledged to publish updated proof of reserves after completing remediation.
Coinbase and Strategy shares also fell in extended US trading, reflecting concern that the incident could weaken investor confidence beyond Binance.
Freezing assets does not immediately return them to Binance.
For Binance customers, the immediate focus remains when withdrawals resume, how much investigators recover and whether the exchange delivers its promised reimbursement.

extraction.body: Binance suffered a record $6.3 billion crypto breach affecting wallets across 10 blockchains. TRM Labs and Chainalysis linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group. Investigators suspect a compromised engineer's laptop enabled unauthorized withdrawals; the full attack path remains unconfirmed. Binance has pledged to cover customer losses after a $6.3 billion security breach that blockchain investigators describe as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, triggering a scramble to freeze stolen assets and contain the market fallout. sources.title: World’s largest crypto exchange hit by suspected North Korean hack in world’s largest heist
passages: Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” pointing out that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist.
North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended withdrawals after hackers broke into its digital wallets and stole $6 billion in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever.

A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim.

Binance said late Thursday that its initial investigation indicated the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Blockchain evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea, according to multiple crypto-tracing firms.

Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment.

extraction.body: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended withdrawals after hackers broke into its digital wallets and stole $6 billion in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever. Binance said late Thursday that its initial investigation indicated the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Blockchain evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea, according to multiple crypto-tracing firms. A team of cryptocurrency firms managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money. Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said on X that the attack was not a “one-click” action, but rather a complex process. The investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual nor found evidence of any wallet private key leak. Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds. The crypto exchange expects withdrawal services to resume by Sunday morning. Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” pointing out that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist. “Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons. “I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds. Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including bitcoin and ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack. CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. CNN has requested comment from the FBI, as well as the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime. In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money. If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes. North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms. A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim. Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry. Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch. However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange, pushing back against any suggestion to the contrary in a spat on X with Elon Musk. Prices of bitcoin and ether, the most widely traded cryptocurrencies, plummeted following news of the Binance breach, but regained some losses to trade about 2-3% lower midday Friday in Hong Kong.

sources.title: ‘Biggest hack in history’: North Korea blamed for huge Binance heist that put crypto market in chaos - The Independent
passages: Hackers have stolen $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in what analysts view as the largest crypto heist in history.
The attack is likely to force investors to rethink the risks of digital assets.
According to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis, North Korea was behind the raid.
TRM Labs said the attackers targeted Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, siphoning most funds within 20 minutes.
Binance stated deposits were unaffected, expecting withdrawals to resume within 48 hours.
TRM said the breach mirrored earlier North Korean heists, including a 2025 hack on Bybit linked by the FBI to Pyongyang.
“It's the biggest hack in history,” said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business.

World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.
Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens ‌had been frozen.
Binance said it collaborated with partners to freeze affected assets, locating around $3 billion so far.
While omitting the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, co-founder Yi He said the exchange would cover “all hacking losses”.
North Korea’s mission in Geneva and its embassy in China did not immediately ⁠respond to requests for comment.

Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring ​reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.
Elsewhere, ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178.
BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that ⁠can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.

An initial investigation suggested the ‌breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm ‌Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance ⁠by an unknown actor.
Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said.
"User funds remain safe," Binance ⁠said in a statement.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.

Binance said it collaborated with partners to freeze affected assets, locating around $3 billion so far. While omitting the status of the remaining $3.3 billion, co-founder Yi He said the exchange would cover “all hacking losses”.
Co-founder Changpeng Zhao, who no longer runs the company, said in a post on X that the incident “looked like a hack.”

Binance stated deposits were unaffected, expecting withdrawals to resume within 48 hours. TRM said the breach mirrored earlier North Korean heists, including a 2025 hack on Bybit linked by the FBI to Pyongyang.

coreStoryFacts.text: The post Binance's $6.3 Billion Hack: North Korea Linked to Record Theft as Exchange Freezes $3 Billion appeared first on ccn.com .
The reported totals reflect different snapshots.
TRM counted approximately $2.7 billion frozen as of 00:30 UTC on October 30, while Binance subsequently reported about $3 billion.
TRM Labs and Chainalysis linked the attack to North Korea's TraderTraitor hacking group.
The world's largest crypto exchange said approximately $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen onchain.
It temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigators examined how an attacker gained access to its withdrawal infrastructure.
Binance's preliminary investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop.
The exchange said the attacker may have used that access to enter a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
Other affected wallets transferred assets through ordinary signed transactions.
Fundstrat's Sean Farrell told CNBC the breach did not currently appear to create a significant solvency threat.
His assessment depended partly on the eventual recovery of frozen assets and Binance's ability to absorb the remaining losses.
TRM estimated the theft at $6.36 billion, with most transfers occurring within roughly 20 minutes.
Withdrawal access now represents a critical test.
A smooth reopening could support confidence in Binance's liquidity, while prolonged restrictions could deepen uncertainty.
Binance said it had found no evidence of leaked wallet private keys.
It has revoked the affected address authorization and promised a technical account once investigators establish the facts.
A batch of 50 previously signed authorizations enabled a malicious contract to take control of a Binance hot wallet and repeatedly drain incoming funds.
It also pledged to publish updated proof of reserves after completing remediation.
Coinbase and Strategy shares also fell in extended US trading, reflecting concern that the incident could weaken investor confidence beyond Binance.
Freezing assets does not immediately return them to Binance.
For Binance customers, the immediate focus remains when withdrawals resume, how much investigators recover and whether the exchange delivers its promised reimbursement.

It temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals while investigators examined how an attacker gained access to its withdrawal infrastructure. extraction.body: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended withdrawals after hackers broke into its digital wallets and stole $6 billion in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever. Binance said late Thursday that its initial investigation indicated the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.” Blockchain evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea, according to multiple crypto-tracing firms. A team of cryptocurrency firms managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money. Binance co-CEO Richard Tend said on X that the attack was not a “one-click” action, but rather a complex process. The investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual nor found evidence of any wallet private key leak. Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds. The crypto exchange expects withdrawal services to resume by Sunday morning. Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” pointing out that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.” Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist. “Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons. “I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds. Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including bitcoin and ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack. CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. CNN has requested comment from the FBI, as well as the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime. In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money. If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes. North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms. A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim. Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry. Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch. However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange, pushing back against any suggestion to the contrary in a spat on X with Elon Musk. Prices of bitcoin and ether, the most widely traded cryptocurrencies, plummeted following news of the Binance breach, but regained some losses to trade about 2-3% lower midday Friday in Hong Kong.

Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds.
CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment.

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces. The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. An adversary could spend months exploiting these relationships to identify vulnerable personnel, develop convincing impersonation attempts, or compromise ongoing investigations.” More than 700 accounts are associated with a group apparently referencing Signal, the encrypted messaging app, nearly all belonging to CBP personnel. More than 200 CBP accounts belong to a group referencing Mobile Fortify, a face-recognition app that immigration agents use to identify people. The group includes field supervisors, special response team operators, and tactical and intelligence agents. Nearly 20 accounts appear to belong to personnel with the Department of Defense, which the administration styles as the Department of War; eight are in a group titled “ICE Tip Line DOW Surge.” About 170 accounts are listed as providing “military processing support” at ICE facilities, and 35 others explicitly identify National Guard members. Dozens of accounts have job titles like “Designated Immigration Officer” and “287(g) Officer,” which mark local law enforcement personnel authorized to carry out some immigration enforcement duties. The records also include roughly 4,400 “associates,” whose jobs range from IT developers and data scientists to nurses and detention officers. Of those, 145 are named as a “contractor” or “high risk contractor.” More than 300 records reference senior titles associated with DHS headquarters, from Noem down through deputy undersecretaries, assistant secretaries, and chiefs of staff to officials overseeing intelligence, technology, biometrics, and privacy. Most records also name a supervisor, which could allow anyone analyzing the dataset to reconstruct reporting relationships across the department.

extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. extraction.body: Data reportedly exposes ICE personnel and officials overseeing covert operations Washington: A nonprofit news leak group said Wednesday it has published data on more than 41,000 employees of the US Department of Homeland Security, including those working on President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts. Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDOS) said it obtained the sensitive information from a "hacktivist group" known as the Department of Peace, which created a tool named Icepick that facilitates detailed searches of employee names, offices and assignments. "This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact," an associated activist, Maia Arson Crimew, said in a DDOS statement. "It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security's organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE," the activist said, refering to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. DHS and ICE have been at the center of an immigration crackdown ordered by Trump at the start of his second term, in January 2025. DDOS cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary." The data "identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers...along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs." The crackdown has seen thousands of undocumented people detained and deported, while US citizens have also been caught up in the dragnet. Last month DHS said it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities" - which are known to limit cooperation between local law enforcement and federal authorities - as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration. The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that Trump's DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months, outpacing the immigration enforcement efforts of his predecessor Joe Biden. It said DHS, including ICE, "completed about 980,000 deportations" in the first 18 months of the second Trump presidential term. Kristi Noem out as homeland security chief: Trump Trump suggests 'softer touch' needed on immigration US official dismisses threat from livestreaming kill Kristi Noem files for divorce from her husband

Washington: A nonprofit news leak group said Wednesday it has published data on more than 41,000 employees of the US Department of Homeland Security, including those working on President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts.

Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDOS) said it obtained the sensitive information from a "hacktivist group" known as the Department of Peace, which created a tool named Icepick that facilitates detailed searches of employee names, offices and assignments.
"This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact," an associated activist, Maia Arson Crimew, said in a DDOS statement.

"It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security's organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE," the activist said, refering to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
DHS and ICE have been at the center of an immigration crackdown ordered by Trump at the start of his second term, in January 2025.
DDOS cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary."

The data "identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers...along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs."
The crackdown has seen thousands of undocumented people detained and deported, while US citizens have also been caught up in the dragnet.

Last month DHS said it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities" - which are known to limit cooperation between local law enforcement and federal authorities - as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration.

The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that Trump's DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months, outpacing the immigration enforcement efforts of his predecessor Joe Biden.
It said DHS, including ICE, "completed about 980,000 deportations" in the first 18 months of the second Trump presidential term.

extraction.body: The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026. The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data for WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.” An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. The leak comes as DHS has aggressively pursued its critics, seeking to unmask anonymous social media users, obtain customer records on protesters, and secure warrants for surveillance tools aimed at reporters. Since the start of the second Trump administration, DHS and the federal government have moved to hide DHS employees’ names and faces. The agency has also expanded its definition of “doxing”—a term that typically refers to publishing someone’s home address and other personal details for malicious purposes—to encompass the publication of basic facts about public employees, like their names and titles. The leak follows a breach in which a group of hackers known as ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen personal information on nearly every FBI employee and their families. The DHS records are searchable on a website crimew built. “I don't think we should let them scare us into not looking into them,” she tells WIRED. “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively,” a Homeland Security spokesperson tells WIRED. “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” The DOJ did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. According to a WIRED analysis of the data, CBP staffers account for more than half of the records. ICE accounts for about 10,000, roughly a third of them in Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative wing. Another 6,200 belong to US Citizenship and Immigration Services, and nearly 1,000 are tied to the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, more than half of them contractors. Altogether, the files cover about a seventh of DHS’s workforce, revealing how DHS is structured, from senior leadership down to individual immigration agents and detention contractors. Like most large organizations, DHS uses permission groups to control access to internal systems, according to the leaked records. Nearly everyone named in the leak has access to at least some of these systems. At HSI, 39 employees across more than a dozen field offices belong to groups whose names include “CUC,” which government court filings say stands for “certified undercover operation.” Another group, apparently based in HSI's St. Paul, Minnesota, area of operations, references "Keyhole," which federal court filings describe as a certified undercover operation that recently funded HSI’s undercover surveillance of Minneapolis protest groups earlier this year. Others reference a “Communications Intercept Center TechOps (CICTO) Program,” a “Title III Intercept Program” for wiretaps, and an “Illicit Sensor Intercept Program (ISIP).” The names of the groups—there are over 55,000 in all—appear to reference tools for accessing immigration court records, pulling data from seized phones, and conducting surveillance. These include Palantir’s Falcon investigative platform and PenLink, which analyzes phone records and social media. Two permission groups, named “Executive Leadership” and “AI Access,” appear to list people given exceptions to DHS's web filter, which blocks some websites for employees. They contain the same 13 people, including former DHS head Kristi Noem; Antoine McCord, the recently departed DHS chief information officer who has returned to defense tech company Anduril; Philip Hegseth, listed as a senior adviser to the DHS secretary and the younger brother of defense secretary Pete Hegseth; and Jayce Krachenfels, listed as a policy adviser, who previously worked as a regional field director for Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. Noem, McCord, Hegseth, and Krachenfels did not respond to a request for comment Other groups named in the leak reference AI tools, including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Microsoft’s Copilot. One, called “Grok.com,” includes eight DHS technology officials, including the department’s former chief information officer and chief data officer. “If authentic and current, this is an extraordinarily valuable intelligence resource for those seeking to penetrate DHS,” says Alexander Leslie, a national security expert at the threat intelligence company Recorded Future. “This dataset becomes way more valuable when correlated with previously compromised information, commercial data, and other intelligence collections. extraction.body: Personally identifiable information belonging to thousands of U.S. Department of Homeland Security employees has been published online after a hacker stole reams of data in a previously undisclosed breach at the government department earlier this year. The breach includes names, job titles, and work contact information, such as email addresses, cell phone numbers, and office locations, of more than 40,000 people who work for the federal department, including border and immigration agents, cybersecurity staffers, and senior department officials. A hacker who goes by the handle Department of Peace claimed they obtained the data from an Okta single sign-on system used by Homeland Security to allow employees and contractors across its various agencies to log in to its central network. The Okta system also contains IT and log-in records associated with the employees’ user account, including details about which systems and internal apps they are permitted to access. More than half of the dataset — some 21,000 records — relate to employees with U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP), who work at airports and other ports of entry. The data also contains records associated with another 10,000 employees of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and its Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) unit, and just under a 1,000 employees who work at U.S. cybersecurity defense agency CISA. Thousands of additional records relate to staff who work at the department’s headquarters and its other agencies, including U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and the Federal Protective Service. “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs,” said Department of Peace in a note left with the data, which TechCrunch has seen. The hacker did not respond to TechCrunch’s email requesting comment and with questions about how the breach was carried out. This is the latest data breach to hit the U.S. government in recent months, following earlier hacks involving the theft of thousands of FBI agents’ personnel records and the personal information of millions of serving and former military service personnel from the Pentagon’s human resources unit . It’s also the second breach involving Homeland Security this year, after the same hacker claimed to have taken thousands of contracts between the department and the private sector, including defense contractors and surveillance vendors. The latest batch of breached data, which appears authentic, offers a rare — albeit incomplete — view into the scale and operations of Homeland Security, whose deportations, arbitrary detentions, and killings of U.S. citizens under its leadership have become a key issue for voters ahead of the upcoming U.S. midterm elections. The stolen Homeland Security data was provided to journalist and hacker maia arson crimew, who then shared a copy with DDoSecrets , a nonprofit collective that hosts leaked datasets in the public interest. TechCrunch verified a portion of the data as authentic by matching the names of several known Homeland Security employees against an offline copy of the database. The thousands of employee directory records appear to have been exfiltrated around mid-August, according to the timestamps on each person’s record. The number of leaked records is equivalent to about one-fifth of Homeland Security’s workforce, which totals around 220,000 staff . It’s unclear whether the vulnerability that allowed the breach has been fixed or if Homeland Security is aware of the data theft. A spokesperson for Homeland Security told TechCrunch after publication: “DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available.” When reached, Okta said it was aware of this report. “Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised,” a spokesperson said. While the leaked data includes identifiable information about agents and officers, the dataset also reveals more about the surveillance technologies and cybersecurity tools that Homeland Security employees may be able to access. Critics have called for investigations into tech companies that fund or provide their technology to ICE. The leaked data contains information about employees’ membership in user groups within the department’s Active Directory, a system that controls access to the department’s internal tools, services, and third-party offerings used for work. Most of the Homeland Security employees in the dataset were members of the user group that had access to Microsoft 365, the tech giant’s cloud service that hosts the agency’s emails and files, as well as user groups for accessing Adobe Acrobat, Citrix, and other typical desktop software. The data also shows that around 4,500 users, including ICE agents and deportation officers, are members of a group called “Headspace_users.” Online therapy provider Headspace previously had an $82,500 federal contract with ICE that ended in 2023 to fund “mental health software required for ERO employees,” a reference to ICE’s deportation unit. A spokesperson for Headspace said the company has not provided any services to DHS or ICE since 2023. Dozens of other user groups reference Penlink , a web surveillance company that makes technology it claims can track the location data of hundreds of millions of mobile devices. Penlink has had a contract with ICE for years. The user groups vary in size, from a handful of users in local Homeland Security offices around the country to more than 2,000 users across ICE’s HSI unit nationally. One group specifically references Penlink PLX, which the company says is used to capture and analyze “real-time intelligence” from phone calls, texts, web activity, and social media. A spokesperson for Penlink did not respond to a request for comment. One user group also includes more than 200 CBP users associated with Mobile Fortify, a facial-recognition app used by both CBP and ICE agents to identify people and verify their information and immigration status . The user groups also include several employees associated with ChatGPT access, including senior DHS officials, as well as other groups associated with investigations into the China-backed hacking groups known as Salt Typhoon and Volt Typhoon. Researchers and public information advocates say that the exposed data could provide valuable leads for investigations into alleged abuses by the Trump administration, such as identifying email addresses of agents that can be used in public records requests under the Freedom of Information Act. “Email addresses and phone numbers are indispensable tools for FOIA researchers, often making the difference between a vague records request that gets stonewalled and one that gets results,” said Ryan Shapiro, the executive director of transparency nonprofit Property of the People. “Given the Trump administration’s contempt for even basic transparency, the need for such tools is urgent,” said Shapiro. DDoSecrets co-founder and journalist Emma Best said that the exposed Homeland Security data will be a “catalyst for investigations, empowering journalists, Congressional inquiries, legal challenges, community action and Freedom of Information Act requests.” Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch.
