extraction.body: Data reportedly exposes ICE personnel and officials overseeing covert operations Washington: A nonprofit news leak group said Wednesday it has published data on more than 41,000 employees of the US Department of Homeland Security, including those working on President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts. Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDOS) said it obtained the sensitive information from a "hacktivist group" known as the Department of Peace, which created a tool named Icepick that facilitates detailed searches of employee names, offices and assignments. "This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact," an associated activist, Maia Arson Crimew, said in a DDOS statement. "It provides an unprecedented look into the Department of Homeland Security's organizational structure, highlighting which people do what work across multiple DHS agencies, including ICE," the activist said, refering to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. DHS and ICE have been at the center of an immigration crackdown ordered by Trump at the start of his second term, in January 2025. DDOS cofounder Emma Best called the leak "extraordinary." The data "identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government's hunt for leakers...along with key personnel in DHS's ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs." The crackdown has seen thousands of undocumented people detained and deported, while US citizens have also been caught up in the dragnet. Last month DHS said it was initiating a "surge in sanctuary cities" - which are known to limit cooperation between local law enforcement and federal authorities - as the Trump administration ramped up its crackdown on immigration. The non-partisan Migration Policy Institute said in a fact sheet that Trump's DHS has expanded its arrests and deportations over the last several months, outpacing the immigration enforcement efforts of his predecessor Joe Biden. It said DHS, including ICE, "completed about 980,000 deportations" in the first 18 months of the second Trump presidential term. passages: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around $6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether -- a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT -- said his firm froze about $1.6 billion "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news.
BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.

The company -- the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes -- said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach", contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around $6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist. The company -- the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes -- said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach", contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance wrote on X. Blockchain investigation firm TRM Labs said it had "high confidence" that the attack was orchestrated by a group of hackers affiliated with North Korea called TraderTraitor. "Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists," TRM said. TraderTraitor is believed to be part of Lazarus Group -- which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for "The Interview," a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Binance confirmed on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion." That is four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform. That heist was attributed at the time to North Korea-backed TraderTraitor. Binance warned the $6.3 billion figure "may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets." It said around $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen. Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses. At about 0900 GMT Friday, Binance said it was on track to resume withdrawals in 45 hours, after announcing earlier that all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended". The company had said on X that initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorized party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions. "We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," it said, promising to share a detailed technical analysis once investigations were complete. But it said later that "subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach." Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether -- a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT -- said his firm froze about $1.6 billion "related to a potential Binance exchange hack." Jeremy Allaire, who runs cryptocurrency platform Circle, said his company had frozen more than $800 million in USDC. USDT and USDC are both "stablecoins," or digital currencies whose value is linked to a traditional currency, the US dollar. The US Department of Justice and the FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform. The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins. Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news. BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent. The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
30, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement."
"We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said.

The company, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses."

extraction.body: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said it had fallen victim to a major hack that hit around $6.3 billion in funds, with about half that amount frozen to prevent a massive theft. The company, the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes, posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses." The company later said on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion." "We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far," it added. That would be four times the amount impacted in what had been the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date: $1.5 billion taken in February last year from the Bybit platform, which was attributed to hackers affiliated with North Korea. At about 0030 GMT on Oct. 30, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been "temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement." "This figure may continue to increase as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company said. The company's statement on X said an initial investigation suggested the hack involved a compromised laptop belonging to a "DevOps engineer," allowing the unauthorized party to access a "service container" and execute unauthorized withdrawal transactions. "We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets," Binance said. For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform. The prices of most major cryptocurrencies fell on news of the cyberattack, except for the stablecoins, which by definition can only fluctuate within tight margins. Thousands of students and workers took to the streets across Italy on Oct. 30, calling for more school funding and relief from the soaring cost of living, amid a high police presence to avert possible clashes. Fixed capital investments in Türkiye’s energy sector are projected to reach 538.3 billion Turkish Liras in 2027, up 29.7 percent his year, according to the 2027 Presidential Annual Program. Victor Osimhen scored twice as Galatasaray beat archrivals Fenerbahçe 2-1 in a heated Istanbul derby on Oct. 26 to move to the top of Türkiye’s Süper Lig, with two players sent off after the final whistle.

sources.title: Crypto exchange Binance confirms $6.3 billion hack, freezes half - Kuwait Times
passages: NEW YORK: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said on Thursday it had been hit by a major hack affecting about $6.3 billion in funds, around half of which has been frozen to prevent theft.

The world’s largest crypto exchange by daily trading volume posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, saying “user funds are completely safe” but also that it would “cover all losses”.
That is four times the previous record for such an attack, the $1.5 billion stolen from the Bybit platform in February last year, which was attributed to hackers linked to North Korea.

Tether chief Paolo Ardoino said his company had frozen about $1.6 billion of its USDT stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”, and Circle chief Jeremy Allaire said his firm had frozen more than $800 million in USDC.
Stablecoins are digital currencies pegged to a traditional currency, in this case the US dollar.
The US Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The figure “may continue to increase” as it works to trace and freeze more assets, it said.
An initial investigation suggested the hackers used a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer” to access a “service container” and carry out unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
“We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising a detailed technical analysis once the investigation is complete.
“It does look like a hack on Binance,” said former chief executive Changpeng Zhao, who remains majority shareholder.
Most major cryptocurrencies fell on the news.

At about 0400 GMT, bitcoin and Ethereum were down 0.8 percent, after falling nearly 5 percent and 6 percent respectively, while Binance’s BNB token was up 2.7 percent after a plunge of nearly 10 percent. — AFP

coreStoryFacts.text: Cryptocurrency platform Binance said Friday it was working to resolve a "complex attack" that affected around $6.3 billion in funds, in what is thought to be the biggest ever crypto heist.
Paolo Ardoino, the boss of Tether -- a company that issues a cryptocurrency known as USDT -- said his firm froze about $1.6 billion "related to a potential Binance exchange hack."
For several hours before Binance confirmed the attack, industry observers said hackers had managed to reach the platform.
Bitcoin and Ethereum plunged nearly five percent and nearly six percent respectively on the news.
BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10 percent.

The company -- the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes -- said investigations had "uncovered additional points of breach", contrary to initial findings that suggested the hack involved a single compromised laptop.
Binance earlier posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses.
The attack on Binance comes as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.

That is four times the previous record for such an attack, the $1.5 billion stolen from the Bybit platform in February last year, which was attributed to hackers linked to North Korea.

At about 0030 GMT on Friday, Binance said all deposits and withdrawals had been “temporarily suspended while our team conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement”. The figure “may continue to increase” as it works to trace and freeze more assets, it said.

An initial investigation suggested the hackers used a compromised laptop belonging to a “DevOps engineer” to access a “service container” and carry out unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said. “We have found no evidence of any private key leaks from wallets,” it said, promising a detailed technical analysis once the investigation is complete. “It does look like a hack on Binance,” said former chief executive Changpeng Zhao, who remains majority shareholder.

Tether chief Paolo Ardoino said his company had frozen about $1.6 billion of its USDT stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”, and Circle chief Jeremy Allaire said his firm had frozen more than $800 million in USDC. Stablecoins are digital currencies pegged to a traditional currency, in this case the US dollar. The US Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Most major cryptocurrencies fell on the news. At about 0400 GMT, bitcoin and Ethereum were down 0.8 percent, after falling nearly 5 percent and 6 percent respectively, while Binance’s BNB token was up 2.7 percent after a plunge of nearly 10 percent. — AFP

They are poisoning our water.” Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine’s most volatile campaign issues. Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers — had Gov. But the fight hasn’t slowed down, with towns across the state adopting temporary moratoriums or putting the question of data center expansion to voters this November. In a September poll of Mainers by UMass Lowell and YouGov, 76 percent of respondents said they oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 percent strongly opposed. Maine’s hotly contested Senate race is set to be the most expensive Senate race per capita that the US has ever seen, with Democrats spending a projected $81 million and Republicans $114 million. Much of that campaign cash has come from the very industry Mainers and rural voters across the country have been fighting for more than a year. The outcome of the race will help determine which party controls the Senate and help shape federal data center and AI policy, impacting data center construction not just for Maine residents, but for the entire country. Cheap land, rich water Maine and other rural states are becoming prime targets for new data centers. While cities run short on land and power, Maine has abundant cheap land, vacant industrial mills and buildings, and ample access to water, thanks to its numerous rivers and waterways. Recognizing the high stakes, major tech companies and private equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals. Molly White, the researcher, writer, and software engineer behind Tech Influence Watch, says that voters are paying a lot of attention to the issue because they connect data centers to rising costs for utilities. As White points out, many Mainers are also already feeling the pinch due to record-high heating oil costs this fall, and “they’re now looking at an election where the question is, is this candidate going to invite a data center to move in next door, and then my electricity prices go up, or the knock-on effects are going to hurt me even more when I’m already in very dire straits?” she said. White launched her site in 2024 to track crypto spending in political races, but has since expanded it to monitor AI and Big Tech investments. White says the playbook that AI and data center backers are using in the midterms is very similar to the one the cryptocurrency industry used in 2024. “There’s a lot going on in this election,” White says, “but I do think it has been a big issue in Maine and across the country, where you’ll go to a political event, you’ll see people asking questions of candidates, and AI keeps coming up. Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.” "“Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.”" - Molly White Data center developers and their political allies often sell rural Maine communities on long-term job creation — a promise economists say rarely materializes. In reality, economic research indicates that most data centers create virtually no net employment once construction is complete. Historically, Maine’s industry has centered around lumber and timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp and paper manufacturing. The timber industry contributed around $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising operating costs have hit it hard, resulting in mill closures and layoffs. Mark Brewer, who chairs the political science department at the University of Maine, says Maine’s history complicates the debate. “Maine has a long history of extractive industries providing jobs,” Brewer says, which allowed Mainers to tolerate these industries despite the state’s environmental focus. With data centers thus far, he says, “the jobs part of it’s not there. Data centers aren’t doing that.” For many rural Mainers, the question is not only whether a data center will bring jobs back, but whether to trust the companies promising them or the government helping make the deal, said Nicholas Jacobs, the director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College in Maine. These residents say they’re concerned about the opaque ownership of these data centers, limited long-term employment, and the risk of wealth being extracted from rural communities. Tech millions fuel Collins’ reelection war chest Tech and AI interests see an ally in Susan Collins, the 73-year-old Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Like most congressional Republicans, she has largely supported data centers and AI, though she has said she believes data centers should be evaluated on an individual basis. Collins has even used her position as head of the Appropriations Committee to secure $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub data center in central Maine, which is designed to bolster localized AI and biotech research. Her stance has brought in a tremendous amount of campaign donations from Big Tech, AI, and data center donors for her reelection bid. Collins’ individual donors include Alex Karp, the cofounder and CEO of Palantir; Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz of VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which heavily backs data centers; and others from Google, Meta, and Microsoft. According to White’s donation tracker, Collins has received $325,644 from AI and crypto donors. Nearly 100 billionaires have donated to Collins’ reelection bid in some form or another. Data centers aren’t doing that.”" - Mark Brewer Super PACs like the Republican Senate Leadership Fund dumped nearly $42 million into ads across Maine. Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund this summer, and has spent around $450 million of his own money to support Republicans in the midterms. Musk’s America PAC has spent around $2.1 million in Maine.

extraction.body: The nationwide backlash against the AI buildout promises to play a decisive role in a handful of Senate races this year, and could in turn determine who will control Congress for the second half of Donald Trump ’s presidency. Evidence is mixed when it comes to which party voters trust on the issue, though Democrats seem to be maintaining a slight advantage. Recent NBC News polling found that they held a 12-point lead when it came to “dealing with data centers ”—32 percent to 20 percent—though 19 percent said both parties were “about the same” and a quarter responded that neither could be trusted. Republicans , however, had a two-point edge on the more general matter of artificial intelligence in a New York Times /Siena poll published last week—within its margin of error. But among voters, opposition to their construction has emerged as one of the only positions drawing bipartisan support this cycle. In June, 64 percent of respondents told a Reuters/Ipsos survey that they disagreed with constructing data centers at scale and pace, and the latest NBC News poll found that the same share of registered voters would be less likely to support a candidate who backs building these facilities in their community. The sleeper issue has become a potentially election-deciding matter, formerly pro-development politicians are now vocal skeptics of an unchecked development push, and campaigns for the House and Senate increasingly read like competitions for who can appear more anti-AI, with Republican strategists telling Newsweek candidates are now “fleeing” from their initial stances on the buildings given alarming levels of local opposition. “Frankly, any incumbent, Republican or Democrat, should be concerned about being tagged as pro-data center,” political strategist Pete Seat told Newsweek. “The loudest voices are being heard, and policy is being made with those voices leading the charge," he said, adding that this trend he says will continue “until the pro-development side can marshal a grassroots army of its own.” Jaymie Scotto Cutaia, founder and CEO of the data center PR firm JSA, told Newsweek that voter concerns about grid capacity, water usage and local community impacts were “resonating with voters across party lines," which in turn "creates an incentive for candidates to adopt increasingly aggressive positions, particularly in closely contested races.” And veteran GOP strategist John Thomas said that, while not nationally a priority on the same level as immigration and the economy, data centers’ political implications appeared to correlate with the presence and scale of a local buildout. Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s latest update , seven races are currently considered “toss ups,” with two that “lean Democrat” meaning a total of nine could be considered close. Of these, the power-infrastructure tracking website Cleanview.co shows that eight have at least one planned data center—i.e., formally proposed or documented in records but not yet operational. This includes closely watched contests like Maine, where the incumbent Republican Susan Collins is taking on the Democrat Troy Jackson, and where three data center projects are currently planned. Alongside Virginia, Texas is leading the data center development push —with over 300 data centers in the works, per Cleanview. And this has now shown signs of becoming a key attack line in the contest between Democratic State Representative James Talarico and his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million linked to the data center industry,” Talarico said in a recent CBS News interview , in which he called Paxton “bought and paid for” by the industry and bragged that he himself receives no center-linked campaign donations. And in Ohio , where 155 data centers are currently planned, Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, recently began running ads which hail the incumbent Senator Jon Husted as the “face of data centers” A memo first published by Axios last month revealed that Republican leadership were concerned that data centers—and the party’s apparent proximity to the industry—were becoming a burden for GOP candidates in the midterms. The memo made specific mention of the Ohio race and Brown’s AI-focused strategy. “If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice—and they will not go near the next one,” the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Experts share this sentiment, though they have expressed doubt that either party had yet secured an advantage in painting themselves as less pro-data center. “I don't think it's a partisan issue,” Douglas Heye, a senior adviser to the Iowa Republican Party, told Newsweek . He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026. However, Republican political consultant Mike Madrid said that examples like Texas show that Republicans are “fleeing from early support of data centers”—a pivot perhaps delayed by Trump’s overt backing of a rapid and nationwide development push. And the party itself has now tried to cast Democrats as, if not more pro-data center, at least less committed to protecting voters from the cost of these facilities. “Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek. Thomas, managing director at the consulting firm Nestpoint, told Newsweek that Republicans should be concerned about the “framing” of the data center conversation rather than AI infrastructure “in general.” “The durable position is require certain conditions, not a ban and not a blank check,” he said. Trump has framed data center development as key to maintaining a lead over China in the “AI race ,” as well as an economic boon for the communities that welcome their construction. Those that don’t, he said in August, will end up “ backwards and poor ”—a sentiment Thomas said candidates should consider toxic if they are to make any inroads with AI-skeptical communities. Even those at the end of the data center backlash acknowledge that these have been poorly sold to the U.S. public. “Data centers have become a political flashpoint because their impacts are intensely local, driving home the old adage that all politics are local,” Brad MacAfee, CEO of the energy infrastructure PR firm KAOH, told Newsweek . “When our politicians mischaracterize rural communities as ‘backwards and poor’ for asking legitimate questions about their power bills, water, land and infrastructure, it only reinforces that divide,” he said. And the traction that anti-data center rhetoric has gained leading into this year’s elections could shape not only the way America votes in November, but also help chart the country’s AI course in 2027 and beyond. “If data centers prove decisive in several races, elected officials in both parties will take notice,” Cutaia told Newsweek . “It would not necessarily stop the AI buildout, but it could slow it, increase development costs and shift investment toward communities and states with clearer regulatory frameworks and stronger public support.” As it stands, however, questions over the environmental and financial cost of powering these buildings mean few voters want to live near them—and that there are fewer politicians now willing to stand behind them. “There’s no constituency for future AI data centers,” said Madrid. “If the politics change the politicians will scramble to catch up. “But at the moment no one wants to touch them.”

And veteran GOP strategist John Thomas said that, while not nationally a priority on the same level as immigration and the economy, data centers’ political implications appeared to correlate with the presence and scale of a local buildout.
Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers.

According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s latest update , seven races are currently considered “toss ups,” with two that “lean Democrat” meaning a total of nine could be considered close. Of these, the power-infrastructure tracking website Cleanview.co shows that eight have at least one planned data center—i.e., formally proposed or documented in records but not yet operational.
This includes closely watched contests like Maine, where the incumbent Republican Susan Collins is taking on the Democrat Troy Jackson, and where three data center projects are currently planned.

Alongside Virginia, Texas is leading the data center development push —with over 300 data centers in the works, per Cleanview. And this has now shown signs of becoming a key attack line in the contest between Democratic State Representative James Talarico and his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

"Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million linked to the data center industry,” Talarico said in a recent CBS News interview , in which he called Paxton “bought and paid for” by the industry and bragged that he himself receives no center-linked campaign donations.

And in Ohio , where 155 data centers are currently planned, Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, recently began running ads which hail the incumbent Senator Jon Husted as the “face of data centers”

A memo first published by Axios last month revealed that Republican leadership were concerned that data centers—and the party’s apparent proximity to the industry—were becoming a burden for GOP candidates in the midterms. The memo made specific mention of the Ohio race and Brown’s AI-focused strategy.

“If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice—and they will not go near the next one,” the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.”
Experts share this sentiment, though they have expressed doubt that either party had yet secured an advantage in painting themselves as less pro-data center.

“I don't think it's a partisan issue,” Douglas Heye, a senior adviser to the Iowa Republican Party, told Newsweek . He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026.

However, Republican political consultant Mike Madrid said that examples like Texas show that Republicans are “fleeing from early support of data centers”—a pivot perhaps delayed by Trump’s overt backing of a rapid and nationwide development push. And the party itself has now tried to cast Democrats as, if not more pro-data center, at least less committed to protecting voters from the cost of these facilities.

“Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek.

Thomas, managing director at the consulting firm Nestpoint, told Newsweek that Republicans should be concerned about the “framing” of the data center conversation rather than AI infrastructure “in general.”
“The durable position is require certain conditions, not a ban and not a blank check,” he said.

Trump has framed data center development as key to maintaining a lead over China in the “AI race ,” as well as an economic boon for the communities that welcome their construction. Those that don’t, he said in August, will end up “ backwards and poor ”—a sentiment Thomas said candidates should consider toxic if they are to make any inroads with AI-skeptical communities.
Even those at the end of the data center backlash acknowledge that these have been poorly sold to the U.S. public.

“Data centers have become a political flashpoint because their impacts are intensely local, driving home the old adage that all politics are local,” Brad MacAfee, CEO of the energy infrastructure PR firm KAOH, told Newsweek .

“When our politicians mischaracterize rural communities as ‘backwards and poor’ for asking legitimate questions about their power bills, water, land and infrastructure, it only reinforces that divide,” he said.

And the traction that anti-data center rhetoric has gained leading into this year’s elections could shape not only the way America votes in November, but also help chart the country’s AI course in 2027 and beyond.
“If data centers prove decisive in several races, elected officials in both parties will take notice,” Cutaia told Newsweek .

“It would not necessarily stop the AI buildout, but it could slow it, increase development costs and shift investment toward communities and states with clearer regulatory frameworks and stronger public support.”

As it stands, however, questions over the environmental and financial cost of powering these buildings mean few voters want to live near them—and that there are fewer politicians now willing to stand behind them.
“There’s no constituency for future AI data centers,” said Madrid. “If the politics change the politicians will scramble to catch up.
“But at the moment no one wants to touch them.”

extraction.body: BANGOR, Maine -- Former state lawmaker and logger Troy Jackson secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Maine on Saturday. He will face longtime GOP Sen. Susan Collins in November in a race that could decide which party controls the Senate. Jackson replaces Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary in June but withdrew from the race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault that Platner has denied. Platner's exit forced Democrats to quickly come up with a never-before-used process to choose a new nominee, which involved more than 600 delegates from across the state gathering in Bangor, about 130 miles (209.21 kilometers) north of Portland, to vote on a new nominee. Jackson won the support of a majority of delegates to clinch the nomination. Jackson's victory was largely expected after his campaign touted that more than 480 delegates selected to go to the convention had promised to vote for him, a progressive who supports Medicare for All and dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Jackson first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat inside Maine's House of Representatives. He lost, but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004, and eventually became the Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024. He came in third while running for governor in this year's Democratic primary election, but had the backing of Platner, U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Our Revolution, the political organization founded by Sanders. THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. AP's earlier story follows below. Maine Democrats on Saturday will choose a new U.S. Senate nominee to face longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a contest that could decide control of the Senate, after Graham Platner dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault. Support has coalesced around former state Senate President Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from rural northern Maine who campaigned alongside Platner during a failed bid for governor and was a favorite among progressives to replace him. "When the people in power refuse to listen, you have to organize, you have to stand in solidarity, together. And you have to make them listen," Jackson said during a speech at a last-minute nominating convention held Saturday. The Maine Democratic Party has been scrambling to choose a new nominee after Platner, who sailed to victory in the Democratic primary in June, was accused by a former girlfriend of sexually assaulting her in 2021. Platner denies the allegation, but quit the race after key supporters called on him to withdraw. Democrats have seen Maine as the party's best opportunity to flip a Senate seat this year because it is a competitive Senate race in a state that President Donald Trump lost in 2024. But defeating Collins won't be easy. The five-term incumbent holds a fundraising advantage, while the new nominee will have less than four months to sell themselves to voters. Maine law gave the state party authority to choose a replacement and required a new nominee to be named by Monday - 99 days before the Nov. 3 election. Maine Democrats' never-before-used process of voting on a new nominee involved more than 600 Democratic delegates gathering in Bangor, about 130 miles (209.21 kilometers) north of Portland. The delegates were elected at county party meetings last weekend. The nominating convention began Saturday morning and was expected to wrap by afternoon. Once Platner dropped out on July 10, a flood of former governor candidates - including Jackson - and others jumped to try to take Platner's place. But by July 19, most had abandoned their bids, with Jackson emerging as the clear favorite. Jackson received early support from progressives who had backed Platner before he dropped out. Our Revolution, the political organization founded nearly a decade ago by Sen. Bernie Sanders, initially backed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate. When Platner left the race, the group rallied behind Jackson. Jackson previously ran Maine operations for Sanders' 2016 presidential bid. This election cycle, Sanders endorsed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate, though the independent senator from Vermont withdrew his support for Platner after the sexual assault allegation. He said he didn't plan to weigh in on which Democrat should replace Platner. Just one other candidate has remained in the race for the Senate nomination - women's health company CEO Saundra Pelletier. She faces long odds against Jackson, who has been a fixture in Maine politics for more than a decade. Jackson's campaign has said more than 480 of the 601 delegates who will be voting at Saturday's convention are committed to supporting him. Jackson has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He also has called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month. Democrats have a narrow path to take back the Senate in November and it's highly unlikely they can do it without a win in Maine. In addition, they need victories in competitive races in North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, and they need to hang on to the seats they already have. That includes open Senate seats in Michigan and Minnesota, where Democratic incumbents are retiring. Maine's Democratic primary was one of the early contests where progressives took on establishment-backed Democrats. While Platner faced several controversies during his campaign, he easily outlasted Gov. Janet Mills, who was backed by Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer but dropped out before the June 9 primary. Platner had backing from Sanders as well as Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. That support disintegrated after the sexual assault allegation early this month. If he becomes the nominee, Jackson will need to convince the state's large independent voting bloc that it's time to replace Collins. Republicans have called Jackson too extreme for Maine voters, and Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are "clearly" in line with socialism. She noted Jackson ran Sanders' first presidential campaign in Maine, adding "He's a Bernie Bro." Jackson would also need to scramble to make up a fundraising gulf against Collins, who has been raising money for months. Federal filings show she has raised more than $16 million so far. Jackson's campaign this week said he raised more than $1 million since jumping into the Senate race. Jackson said Saturday he believes his team is up to the task.

extraction.body: Janet Mills said Friday that she hasn’t decided whether to sign a bill passed by the Legislature to impose a statewide moratorium on new data centers, outlining her critique of the legislation. Read it very carefully,” Mills, a Democrat, said in a wide-ranging interview with NBC News, adding that it doesn’t contain a “carveout” she wanted for a project in the struggling town of Jay in order to boost jobs. Mills’ decision is being closely watched: The first-of-its-kind bill comes amid a national debate that features growing local opposition to the huge, energy-hungry structures that power the growing and disruptive artificial intelligence industry. The measure, passed earlier this week, would impose a moratorium on new data centers in Maine until the fall of 2027. Mills has 10 days to decide whether to sign the bill, veto it or otherwise allow it to become law without her taking action. “I have already expressed publicly concerns for the project that’s proposed in Jay, Maine, which has lost actually two paper mills in that community in the last couple years,” Mills said. “It was probably one of the worst days of my tenure as governor, when in the middle of the pandemic and the George Floyd demonstrations, protests, we saw a video of the digesters in Jay falling over,” she added. Where are the locusts?” “And that mill obviously closed and they lost all the jobs they had, pretty much other than service jobs, and those people deserve a good look at what that data center could do for the for the community. So I have said that I would want a carveout for Jay,” she continued. “I’m also concerned about what data centers have done in other states — consumption of electricity and water usage, those kinds of things,” Mills said. “This one is right on the Androscoggin River, and that paper mill once used 40-something million gallons of water each day. So I’m looking at the comparison there, and whether or not it’s viable.” Asked if she might veto the bill and ask the Legislature for a rewrite, Mills said it would be “difficult at this stage of the game.” Lawmakers only “come back for one day,” she said, “for veto day.”

passages: Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers.
“If data centers prove decisive in several races, elected officials in both parties will take notice,” Cutaia told Newsweek .

Jaymie Scotto Cutaia, founder and CEO of the data center PR firm JSA, told Newsweek that voter concerns about grid capacity, water usage and local community impacts were “resonating with voters across party lines," which in turn "creates an incentive for candidates to adopt increasingly aggressive positions, particularly in closely contested races.”

“Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek.

And the traction that anti-data center rhetoric has gained leading into this year’s elections could shape not only the way America votes in November, but also help chart the country’s AI course in 2027 and beyond.

The sleeper issue has become a potentially election-deciding matter, formerly pro-development politicians are now vocal skeptics of an unchecked development push, and campaigns for the House and Senate increasingly read like competitions for who can appear more anti-AI, with Republican strategists telling Newsweek candidates are now “fleeing” from their initial stances on the buildings given alarming levels of local opposition.

extraction.body: The nationwide backlash against the AI buildout promises to play a decisive role in a handful of Senate races this year, and could in turn determine who will control Congress for the second half of Donald Trump ’s presidency. Evidence is mixed when it comes to which party voters trust on the issue, though Democrats seem to be maintaining a slight advantage. Recent NBC News polling found that they held a 12-point lead when it came to “dealing with data centers ”—32 percent to 20 percent—though 19 percent said both parties were “about the same” and a quarter responded that neither could be trusted. Republicans , however, had a two-point edge on the more general matter of artificial intelligence in a New York Times /Siena poll published last week—within its margin of error. But among voters, opposition to their construction has emerged as one of the only positions drawing bipartisan support this cycle. In June, 64 percent of respondents told a Reuters/Ipsos survey that they disagreed with constructing data centers at scale and pace, and the latest NBC News poll found that the same share of registered voters would be less likely to support a candidate who backs building these facilities in their community. The sleeper issue has become a potentially election-deciding matter, formerly pro-development politicians are now vocal skeptics of an unchecked development push, and campaigns for the House and Senate increasingly read like competitions for who can appear more anti-AI, with Republican strategists telling Newsweek candidates are now “fleeing” from their initial stances on the buildings given alarming levels of local opposition. “Frankly, any incumbent, Republican or Democrat, should be concerned about being tagged as pro-data center,” political strategist Pete Seat told Newsweek. “The loudest voices are being heard, and policy is being made with those voices leading the charge," he said, adding that this trend he says will continue “until the pro-development side can marshal a grassroots army of its own.” Jaymie Scotto Cutaia, founder and CEO of the data center PR firm JSA, told Newsweek that voter concerns about grid capacity, water usage and local community impacts were “resonating with voters across party lines," which in turn "creates an incentive for candidates to adopt increasingly aggressive positions, particularly in closely contested races.” And veteran GOP strategist John Thomas said that, while not nationally a priority on the same level as immigration and the economy, data centers’ political implications appeared to correlate with the presence and scale of a local buildout. Given this, Newsweek charted the tight Senate races that are taking place in states with significant numbers of planned data centers. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report’s latest update , seven races are currently considered “toss ups,” with two that “lean Democrat” meaning a total of nine could be considered close. Of these, the power-infrastructure tracking website Cleanview.co shows that eight have at least one planned data center—i.e., formally proposed or documented in records but not yet operational. This includes closely watched contests like Maine, where the incumbent Republican Susan Collins is taking on the Democrat Troy Jackson, and where three data center projects are currently planned. Alongside Virginia, Texas is leading the data center development push —with over 300 data centers in the works, per Cleanview. And this has now shown signs of becoming a key attack line in the contest between Democratic State Representative James Talarico and his Republican rival, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. "Ken Paxton has taken nearly half a million linked to the data center industry,” Talarico said in a recent CBS News interview , in which he called Paxton “bought and paid for” by the industry and bragged that he himself receives no center-linked campaign donations. And in Ohio , where 155 data centers are currently planned, Senate candidate Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, recently began running ads which hail the incumbent Senator Jon Husted as the “face of data centers” A memo first published by Axios last month revealed that Republican leadership were concerned that data centers—and the party’s apparent proximity to the industry—were becoming a burden for GOP candidates in the midterms. The memo made specific mention of the Ohio race and Brown’s AI-focused strategy. “If [Husted] loses and data centers get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice—and they will not go near the next one,” the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote. “This has become a sleeper issue for the entire election cycle.” Experts share this sentiment, though they have expressed doubt that either party had yet secured an advantage in painting themselves as less pro-data center. “I don't think it's a partisan issue,” Douglas Heye, a senior adviser to the Iowa Republican Party, told Newsweek . He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026. However, Republican political consultant Mike Madrid said that examples like Texas show that Republicans are “fleeing from early support of data centers”—a pivot perhaps delayed by Trump’s overt backing of a rapid and nationwide development push. And the party itself has now tried to cast Democrats as, if not more pro-data center, at least less committed to protecting voters from the cost of these facilities. “Republicans are building the AI infrastructure America needs while ensuring companies are paying their own way, shielding families from higher utility bills, and safeguarding local water and natural resources,” Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee, told Newsweek. Thomas, managing director at the consulting firm Nestpoint, told Newsweek that Republicans should be concerned about the “framing” of the data center conversation rather than AI infrastructure “in general.” “The durable position is require certain conditions, not a ban and not a blank check,” he said. Trump has framed data center development as key to maintaining a lead over China in the “AI race ,” as well as an economic boon for the communities that welcome their construction. Those that don’t, he said in August, will end up “ backwards and poor ”—a sentiment Thomas said candidates should consider toxic if they are to make any inroads with AI-skeptical communities. Even those at the end of the data center backlash acknowledge that these have been poorly sold to the U.S. public. “Data centers have become a political flashpoint because their impacts are intensely local, driving home the old adage that all politics are local,” Brad MacAfee, CEO of the energy infrastructure PR firm KAOH, told Newsweek . “When our politicians mischaracterize rural communities as ‘backwards and poor’ for asking legitimate questions about their power bills, water, land and infrastructure, it only reinforces that divide,” he said. And the traction that anti-data center rhetoric has gained leading into this year’s elections could shape not only the way America votes in November, but also help chart the country’s AI course in 2027 and beyond. “If data centers prove decisive in several races, elected officials in both parties will take notice,” Cutaia told Newsweek . “It would not necessarily stop the AI buildout, but it could slow it, increase development costs and shift investment toward communities and states with clearer regulatory frameworks and stronger public support.” As it stands, however, questions over the environmental and financial cost of powering these buildings mean few voters want to live near them—and that there are fewer politicians now willing to stand behind them. “There’s no constituency for future AI data centers,” said Madrid. “If the politics change the politicians will scramble to catch up. “But at the moment no one wants to touch them.”

He pointed to the fact that the Republican governor of Texas, Greg Abbott, has been among the most notable buildout skeptics both rhetorically and legislatively in 2026.

Susan Collins in November in a race that could decide which party controls the Senate. Jackson replaces Graham Platner, who won the Democratic primary in June but withdrew from the race earlier this month following an allegation of sexual assault that Platner has denied. Platner's exit forced Democrats to quickly come up with a never-before-used process to choose a new nominee, which involved more than 600 delegates from across the state gathering in Bangor, about 130 miles (209.21 kilometers) north of Portland, to vote on a new nominee. Jackson won the support of a majority of delegates to clinch the nomination. Jackson's victory was largely expected after his campaign touted that more than 480 delegates selected to go to the convention had promised to vote for him, a progressive who supports Medicare for All and dismantling Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Jackson first ran for office as a Republican in 2000 when he sought a seat inside Maine's House of Representatives. He lost, but won two years later when he ran as an independent. He switched to the Democratic Party in 2004, and eventually became the Maine Senate president before leaving the statehouse in 2024. He came in third while running for governor in this year's Democratic primary election, but had the backing of Platner, U.S. Sen. Maine Democrats on Saturday will choose a new U.S. Senate nominee to face longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins in a contest that could decide control of the Senate, after Graham Platner dropped out of the race following an allegation of sexual assault. Support has coalesced around former state Senate President Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from rural northern Maine who campaigned alongside Platner during a failed bid for governor and was a favorite among progressives to replace him. "When the people in power refuse to listen, you have to organize, you have to stand in solidarity, together. And you have to make them listen," Jackson said during a speech at a last-minute nominating convention held Saturday. The Maine Democratic Party has been scrambling to choose a new nominee after Platner, who sailed to victory in the Democratic primary in June, was accused by a former girlfriend of sexually assaulting her in 2021. Platner denies the allegation, but quit the race after key supporters called on him to withdraw. Democrats have seen Maine as the party's best opportunity to flip a Senate seat this year because it is a competitive Senate race in a state that President Donald Trump lost in 2024. But defeating Collins won't be easy. The five-term incumbent holds a fundraising advantage, while the new nominee will have less than four months to sell themselves to voters. Maine law gave the state party authority to choose a replacement and required a new nominee to be named by Monday - 99 days before the Nov. 3 election. Maine Democrats' never-before-used process of voting on a new nominee involved more than 600 Democratic delegates gathering in Bangor, about 130 miles (209.21 kilometers) north of Portland. The delegates were elected at county party meetings last weekend. The nominating convention began Saturday morning and was expected to wrap by afternoon. Once Platner dropped out on July 10, a flood of former governor candidates - including Jackson - and others jumped to try to take Platner's place. But by July 19, most had abandoned their bids, with Jackson emerging as the clear favorite. Jackson received early support from progressives who had backed Platner before he dropped out. Our Revolution, the political organization founded nearly a decade ago by Sen. Bernie Sanders, initially backed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate. When Platner left the race, the group rallied behind Jackson. Jackson previously ran Maine operations for Sanders' 2016 presidential bid. This election cycle, Sanders endorsed Jackson for governor and Platner for Senate, though the independent senator from Vermont withdrew his support for Platner after the sexual assault allegation. He said he didn't plan to weigh in on which Democrat should replace Platner. Just one other candidate has remained in the race for the Senate nomination - women's health company CEO Saundra Pelletier. She faces long odds against Jackson, who has been a fixture in Maine politics for more than a decade. Jackson's campaign has said more than 480 of the 601 delegates who will be voting at Saturday's convention are committed to supporting him. Jackson has supported progressive positions such as Medicare for All. He also has called for the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, whose presence in Maine has been hotly debated since an agent killed a driver in the state earlier this month. Democrats have a narrow path to take back the Senate in November and it's highly unlikely they can do it without a win in Maine. In addition, they need victories in competitive races in North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, and they need to hang on to the seats they already have. That includes open Senate seats in Michigan and Minnesota, where Democratic incumbents are retiring. Maine's Democratic primary was one of the early contests where progressives took on establishment-backed Democrats. While Platner faced several controversies during his campaign, he easily outlasted Gov. Janet Mills, who was backed by Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer but dropped out before the June 9 primary. Platner had backing from Sanders as well as Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren. That support disintegrated after the sexual assault allegation early this month. If he becomes the nominee, Jackson will need to convince the state's large independent voting bloc that it's time to replace Collins. Republicans have called Jackson too extreme for Maine voters, and Collins said earlier this week that she knows Jackson well and that his positions are "clearly" in line with socialism. She noted Jackson ran Sanders' first presidential campaign in Maine, adding "He's a Bernie Bro." Jackson would also need to scramble to make up a fundraising gulf against Collins, who has been raising money for months. Federal filings show she has raised more than $16 million so far. Jackson's campaign this week said he raised more than $1 million since jumping into the Senate race. Jackson said Saturday he believes his team is up to the task.

extraction.body: Janet Mills said Friday that she hasn’t decided whether to sign a bill passed by the Legislature to impose a statewide moratorium on new data centers, outlining her critique of the legislation. Read it very carefully,” Mills, a Democrat, said in a wide-ranging interview with NBC News, adding that it doesn’t contain a “carveout” she wanted for a project in the struggling town of Jay in order to boost jobs. Mills’ decision is being closely watched: The first-of-its-kind bill comes amid a national debate that features growing local opposition to the huge, energy-hungry structures that power the growing and disruptive artificial intelligence industry. The measure, passed earlier this week, would impose a moratorium on new data centers in Maine until the fall of 2027. Mills has 10 days to decide whether to sign the bill, veto it or otherwise allow it to become law without her taking action. “I have already expressed publicly concerns for the project that’s proposed in Jay, Maine, which has lost actually two paper mills in that community in the last couple years,” Mills said. “It was probably one of the worst days of my tenure as governor, when in the middle of the pandemic and the George Floyd demonstrations, protests, we saw a video of the digesters in Jay falling over,” she added. Where are the locusts?” “And that mill obviously closed and they lost all the jobs they had, pretty much other than service jobs, and those people deserve a good look at what that data center could do for the for the community. So I have said that I would want a carveout for Jay,” she continued. “I’m also concerned about what data centers have done in other states — consumption of electricity and water usage, those kinds of things,” Mills said. “This one is right on the Androscoggin River, and that paper mill once used 40-something million gallons of water each day. So I’m looking at the comparison there, and whether or not it’s viable.” Asked if she might veto the bill and ask the Legislature for a rewrite, Mills said it would be “difficult at this stage of the game.” Lawmakers only “come back for one day,” she said, “for veto day.”

SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended an exhibition devoted to drones and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology, state media reported Friday, as his military escalates threats against South Korea and the U.S. Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to strengthen conventional and nuclear capabilities to counter what he calls U.S.-led security threats. It's unclear how far North Korea's drone program has progressed. Experts say Kim's troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine likely gained experience in drone warfare from Russian forces and their own battlefield experiences. The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Kim visited the exhibition Thursday, viewing attack drones and other models that it said show recent achievements in drone technology. In a speech there, Kim announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said. South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it appeared to be North Korea's first exhibition exclusively dedicated to drones. South Korean media reported the exhibition displayed more than 30 kinds of drones, including stealth drones and first-person-view attack drones. In an analysis for the North Korea-focused 38 North website in September 2025, analyst Martyn Williams said the country’s drone program dates back to at least 2011 and that “further drone development and deployment should be expected as the country works to enhance preparedness for modern warfare.” “The use of drones has been critical in the wars currently being fought in Europe and the Middle East. This trend is likely to ring true for future conflicts — a lesson that all countries are learning, including North Korea,” Williams wrote. South Korea’s state-run Institute for National Security Strategy said in a report last year that Russian assistance could help North Korea overcome technological and industrial limitations on its drone program. To mark the event, KCNA said North Korea tested various drones, missiles and 600 mm-caliber ultraprecision multiple rocket launchers. KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons and clenching his fist while his teenage daughter stood beside him and clapped. South Korea's spy agency believes the girl, reportedly about 13, is Kim's designated heir. South Korea's military said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off the North's east coast Thursday. Tensions between the two Koreas have been high since mine blasts at their border last month wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked. Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border. North Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday condemned a joint U.S.-South Korea air exercise as “provocative” and warned it was increasing the danger of an armed conflict. South Korea's military has said the two-week biannual Freedom Flag drill was to run until Nov. 6 and was meant to improve combined operational capabilities. It said fighter jets, helicopters and drones would take part. North Korea pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim. Meanwhile, Switzerland’s Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday for the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang and to meet North Korean officials. He is traveling on to South Korea on Friday. SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korean leader Kim Jong Un attended an exhibition devoted to drones and called for rapidly expanding the country’s drone technology, state media reported Friday, as his military escalates threats against South Korea and the U.S.
Acquiring advanced drones is a top priority for Kim, who now wants to strengthen conventional and nuclear capabilities to counter what he calls U.S.-led security threats.

It's unclear how far North Korea's drone program has progressed. Experts say Kim's troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine likely gained experience in drone warfare from Russian forces and their own battlefield experiences.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Kim visited the exhibition Thursday, viewing attack drones and other models that it said show recent achievements in drone technology. In a speech there, Kim announced unspecified steps needed to “rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology,” KCNA said.

South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it appeared to be North Korea's first exhibition exclusively dedicated to drones. South Korean media reported the exhibition displayed more than 30 kinds of drones, including stealth drones and first-person-view attack drones.

In an analysis for the North Korea-focused 38 North website in September 2025, analyst Martyn Williams said the country’s drone program dates back to at least 2011 and that “further drone development and deployment should be expected as the country works to enhance preparedness for modern warfare.”

“The use of drones has been critical in the wars currently being fought in Europe and the Middle East. This trend is likely to ring true for future conflicts — a lesson that all countries are learning, including North Korea,” Williams wrote.

South Korea’s state-run Institute for National Security Strategy said in a report last year that Russian assistance could help North Korea overcome technological and industrial limitations on its drone program.
To mark the event, KCNA said North Korea tested various drones, missiles and 600 mm-caliber ultraprecision multiple rocket launchers.

KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons and clenching his fist while his teenage daughter stood beside him and clapped. South Korea's spy agency believes the girl, reportedly about 13, is Kim's designated heir.
South Korea's military said it detected the launches of about 10 short-range ballistic missiles off the North's east coast Thursday.

Tensions between the two Koreas have been high since mine blasts at their border last month wounded three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.

North Korea's Defense Ministry on Friday condemned a joint U.S.-South Korea air exercise as “provocative” and warned it was increasing the danger of an armed conflict. South Korea's military has said the two-week biannual Freedom Flag drill was to run until Nov. 6 and was meant to improve combined operational capabilities. It said fighter jets, helicopters and drones would take part.

North Korea pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with U.S. President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.

Meanwhile, Switzerland’s Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday for the reopening of Switzerland’s diplomatic office in Pyongyang and to meet North Korean officials. He is traveling on to South Korea on Friday.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for rapidly expanding the country's drone technology and observed tests of various weapons, state media reported Friday, as his nation remains embroiled in a standoff with rival South Korea along their heavily fortified border.
To mark the event, KCNA said that North Korea later conducted test-launches of various drones, missiles and weapons from the 600 mm-calibre ultra-precision multiple rocket launchers.

In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim.
Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border.
Seoul accused North Korea of burying the mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology.

The North's official Korean Central News Agency said that Kim on Thursday visited an exhibition of a variety of attack and other drones that show recent achievements in the field of unmanned aeronautical technology.
KCNA photos showed Kim watching soaring weapons or him clenching his fist while his teenage daughter was clapping her hands beside him.

South Korea's spy agency assesses that the girl, reportedly about 13, is likely Kim's heir. Last week, North Korea threatened to resume propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and place new weapons systems along the border. North Korea has pulled out of talks with the U.S. and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomacy with President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has dialed up weapons testing activities in a likely attempt to boost its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after Trump expressed his eagerness to restore talks with Kim. Kim has recently taken steps to cement ties with China, North Korea's economic pipeline, after years of prioritizing ties with Russia, including by sending troops and ammunition to support its war against Ukraine.

passages: SINGAPORE/TOKYO Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets.

TRM said the attackers were able to order wallets that Binance uses to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to North Korea.

World Liberty Financial said it ​worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder ​Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said.

BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to CoinGecko, while shaky ​confidence ​hit listed crypto exchange shares.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, ​has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website.
Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses.
"This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance ‌said in a post on X.
"Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said.
Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach.

Mark Karpeles, former chief of defunct Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox, which collapsed a dozen years ago after $500 million in bitcoin was stolen, said attackers probably accessed private keys for at least two Binance wallets.
"Binance appears to have split its assets across multiple systems, ensuring a hack can only affect a part of the assets, but even so a single hack is a large loss," he said.
"It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said as crypto prices fell broadly.

An initial investigation suggested the breach ‌may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.

extraction.body: By Ankur Banerjee, Rocky Swift and Summer Zhen SINGAPORE/TOKYO Oct 30 (Reuters) - Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in a record theft that analysts pinned on North Korea and said could shake faith in digital assets. Cryptocurrency prices fell on the news, while Binance halted withdrawals and said it would cover the losses. About half the stolen assets were quickly frozen ‌by stablecoin issuers such as Tether, Circle and the Trump-backed World Liberty Financial. "This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it," Binance ‌said in a post on X. The exchange said customer funds were safe and that it was working with partners to freeze some of the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It expects to resume withdrawal services in the next 45 hours. It did not mention ​the status of the remaining $3.3 billion. Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, a $1 billion bitcoin reserve designed to protect customer assets in the event of security breaches, according to its website. Co-CEO Teng said that "and company funds" would cover losses. The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes beginning late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous large attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis. TRM said the attackers were able to order wallets that Binance uses to empty into hacker-controlled wallets, mirroring a 2025 heist at crypto exchange Bybit, which the US Federal Bureau of Investigation attributed to North Korea. "TRM attributes the attack to ... North Korea's elite hacking unit," the firm said in ‌an analysis of the hack posted to its website. Both TRM and Chainalysis ⁠said they were highly confident North Korea was responsible. North Korea routinely denies that. Its mission in Geneva and embassy in China did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment. "Your money ⁠is safe and we're covering every loss," Teng said on X. "Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual." "It's the biggest hack in history," Aravind Srinivasan at market maker GSR said as crypto prices fell broadly. Bitcoin hit a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178 before markets stabilised. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to CoinGecko, while shaky ​confidence ​hit listed crypto exchange shares. Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global, which said it was unaffected, slid 4.8%, while those of bitcoin buyer ​Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading. An initial investigation suggested the breach ‌may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance's engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said. "Our security team is tracing the full attack path through the compromised computer which may be the entry point of the incident," Binance said. Later, the company added it had uncovered additional points of breach. Mark Karpeles, former chief of defunct Tokyo-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox, which collapsed a dozen years ago after $500 million in bitcoin was stolen, said attackers probably accessed private keys for at least two Binance wallets. "Binance appears to have split its assets across multiple systems, ensuring a hack can only affect a part of the assets, but even so a single hack is a large loss," he said. Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for the crypto sector, which had already been under pressure ‌due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said. "It may further dampen risk appetite and ​prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong ​Kong. Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, ​has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of its 2025 annual report. Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets ‌linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million. World Liberty Financial said it ​worked with custodian BitGo to freeze funds, and Binance co-founder ​Yi He said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen. Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's ​vulnerability to hackers. "The broader credit and industry implications will depend on the ultimate ‌losses, affected counterparties, asset recovery, and importantly, whether the incident leads to wider disruption or loss of confidence across the digital-asset ecosystem," said Cristiano Ventricelli, vice president, digital assets at Moody's Ratings.
